lead: A slab cast monolithically with a beam acts as a flange in compression. The result is a T-section when slab lies on both sides and an L-section at an edge. The flange adds a wide concrete compression area, so the beam carries more moment than a rectangular beam of the same web width. Shear lag means only an effective width bf is used. Designers meet this in building floors, where beams support slabs. The chapter shows how to find bf, test whether the neutral axis lies in the flange, and compute tension steel.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for the rectangular stress block and Unit 4 for slab behaviour.

blocks.text: Concrete cast on top of a beam does not stop at the beam face. It continues into the slab. When the beam bends sagging, the slab near the beam is in compression. A T-beam has slab on both sides; an L-beam has slab on one side. The slab is the flange and the beam below is the web.

The flange gives a wide compression area. A flanged beam carries more moment than a rectangular beam of web width b<sub>w</sub> for the same depth and steel. The flange helps only in compression. If the slab lies on the tension side, as over a support in a continuous beam, ignore it.
The slab and beam must be cast monolithically. A precast slab simply resting on a beam does not form a T-section unless shear connection is provided.

Use effective flange width b<sub>f</sub>. Shear lag makes stress fall away from the web, so only a limited slab width is effective. Symbols: b<sub>w</sub> is web breadth; D<sub>f</sub> is flange thickness; b<sub>f</sub> is effective flange width; L<sub>0</sub> is distance between points of zero bending moment. For a simply supported beam, L<sub>0</sub> is the effective span.

IS 456 gives upper limits. For a T-beam: b<sub>f</sub> ≤ b<sub>w</sub> + 2D<sub>f</sub> + L<sub>0</sub>/6, and b<sub>f</sub> ≤ b<sub>w</sub> + clear spacing between beams. For an L-beam: b<sub>f</sub> ≤ b<sub>w</sub> + D<sub>f</sub> + L<sub>0</sub>/12, and b<sub>f</sub> ≤ b<sub>w</sub> + half the clear spacing to the next beam. The smaller value governs.

The spacing limit exists because the slab can be shared only up to midspan between beams; beyond that it belongs to the next beam. For continuous T-beams, L<sub>0</sub> is the distance between points of contraflexure, not always the full span. A T-section and an L-section are both flanged beams; the slab is the flange and the rib is the web.
Never take the whole slab width. A wide b<sub>f</sub> looks safe but gives wrong steel and unsafe checks.

Begin by assuming the neutral axis lies in the flange: x<sub>u</sub> ≤ D<sub>f</sub>. Then concrete compression is a rectangle of width b<sub>f</sub>, and the section is a singly reinforced rectangular beam of width b<sub>f</sub>.

blocks.where: M<sub>u</sub> is factored moment in N·mm; f<sub>ck</sub> concrete strength in N/mm²; b<sub>f</sub> effective flange width in mm; x<sub>u</sub> neutral axis depth in mm; d effective depth in mm.

blocks.text: Solve the quadratic for x<sub>u</sub>. If x<sub>u</sub> ≤ D<sub>f</sub>, the assumption holds. Tension steel A<sub>st</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> x<sub>u</sub> / (0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), where f<sub>y</sub> is steel yield strength. Also check x<sub>u</sub> ≤ x<sub>u,max</sub>; for Fe 415 steel, x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.48.

If x<sub>u</sub> > D<sub>f</sub>, the neutral axis is in the web. Split concrete force into web and flange overhangs. Web force C<sub>w</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>w</sub> x<sub>u</sub>, lever arm d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>. Flange overhang force C<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> (b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>) D<sub>f</sub>. When 0.42x<sub>u</sub> ≥ D<sub>f</sub>, its lever arm is d − D<sub>f</sub>/2. Then M<sub>u</sub> = C<sub>w</sub>(d − 0.42x<sub>u</sub>) + C<sub>f</sub>(d − D<sub>f</sub>/2), and A<sub>st</sub> = (C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>f</sub>)/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>). If 0.42x<sub>u</sub> < D<sub>f</sub>, the rectangular stress block does not cover the full flange depth. Replace D<sub>f</sub> by 0.42x<sub>u</sub> in C<sub>f</sub>, so C<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> (b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>)(0.42x<sub>u</sub>), and the lever arm becomes d − 0.42x<sub>u</sub>/2 = d − 0.21x<sub>u</sub>. If 0.42x<sub>u</sub> ≥ D<sub>f</sub>, use D<sub>f</sub> itself with lever arm d − D<sub>f</sub>/2.
If xu exceeds xu,max, add compression steel as in Chapter 2.3 or increase the depth. Design aids in Chapter 2.5 speed the rectangular step.

examples.question: A T-beam has bf = 1000 mm, bw = 300 mm, Df = 100 mm, d = 500 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm² and Mu = 250 kN·m. Check whether xu lies within the flange and find Ast.
steps: Assume xu ≤ Df = 100 mm. Use rectangular width bf = 1000 mm.
Write Mu = 0.36 fck bf xu (d − 0.42 xu). Substitute: 250 × 10⁶ = 0.36 × 25 × 1000 × xu × (500 − 0.42 xu).
Check assumption: xu = 58.42 mm < Df = 100 mm. The neutral axis lies inside the flange.
Check ductility: xu/d = 58.42/500 = 0.117 < 0.48 for Fe 415. The section is under-reinforced.
Provide 4 bars of 22 mm diameter: area = 4 × 380.13 = 1520.5 mm², which is more than 1456.32 mm².
examples.answer: xu = 58.42 mm lies within the 100 mm flange, so design as a rectangular beam of width 1000 mm; Ast = 1456.32 mm².
examples.check:
import math
fck = 25.0
fy = 415.0
bf = 1000.0
bw = 300.0
Df = 100.0
d = 500.0
Mu = 250e6
A = 0.36 * fck * bf * 0.42
B = -0.36 * fck * bf * d
C = Mu
disc = B * B - 4 * A * C
xu = (-B - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * A)
Ast = 0.36 * fck * bf * xu / (0.87 * fy)
print(f'{xu:.2f}')
print(f'{Ast:.2f}')

traps: Using web width bw when the neutral axis lies inside the flange; the correct width is bf.
Taking the whole slab width as bf and forgetting the IS 456 limits from span and clear spacing.
Using the flange when the slab is in tension, such as over a support in a continuous beam.
In a T-section stress block, counting the full width bf in the flange overhang term instead of (bf − bw), which double-counts the web.
Forgetting to check xu ≤ xu,max; a flanged beam can still be over-reinforced even when the flange is in compression.

quiz.q: What does bf mean in a flanged beam?
quiz.a: bf is the effective flange width: the limited slab width taken as acting with the web in compression.

quiz.q: Why is the full slab width not used as the flange width?
quiz.a: Shear lag makes slab stress fall away from the web. Only a limited width near the web develops useful compression, so IS 456 limits bf by span, flange thickness and clear spacing.

quiz.q: A T-beam has bw = 300 mm, Df = 100 mm, L0 = 6000 mm and clear spacing between beams = 2700 mm. Find bf.
quiz.a: Span limit: bw + 2Df + L0/6 = 300 + 200 + 1000 = 1500 mm. Spacing limit: bw + clear spacing = 300 + 2700 = 3000 mm. The smaller value governs, so bf = 1500 mm.

quiz.q: A flanged beam has Df = 100 mm and a trial xu = 120 mm. Which analysis path applies?
quiz.a: xu > Df, so the neutral axis is in the web. Use the T-section stress block with web force plus flange overhang force, not a rectangle of width bf.

quiz.q: A designer uses bw instead of bf for a beam whose xu is 60 mm and Df is 100 mm. What error results?
quiz.a: The compression area is underestimated. The calculated xu and Ast become too large, and the section is designed uneconomically; the correct path is a rectangular beam of width bf because xu ≤ Df.

quiz.q: Why is a flange in tension ignored?
quiz.a: Concrete is weak in tension and cracks. Only the steel carries tension, so a slab on the tension side does not add flexural compression capacity.

quiz.q: For a continuous T-beam, why may L0 be less than the full span?
quiz.a: L0 is the distance between points of zero bending moment. Near supports, negative moment changes sign at points of contraflexure, so the distance between those points is used.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, flanged-beam checks appear in building-floor software and in bridge deck analysis, where effective width rules differ between codes. Shear in flanged beams is more complex because the flange carries part of the shear flow; that belongs to Unit 3. Researchers study shear lag and wide-flange effects using shell models.
